add_eyes.name: Marc de Montifaud (Marie-Amélie Chartroule de Montifaud)
add_eyes.role: Writer and art critic, aged about 25, publishing under a male pen-name
add_eyes.where: Paris; the rooms at 35 boulevard des Capucines
add_eyes.vantage_label: a woman critic in the rooms, behind a man's name
add_eyes.authenticity: 'Exposition du boulevard des Capucines', L'Artiste, May 1874. The day is cited as 1 May in some bibliographies and 9 May in the Degas catalogue raisonné. The content here follows secondary accounts; the issue itself was not consulted.
add_eyes.bio: Montifaud wrote art criticism and fiction under a man's name. She is the woman most often named among the critics of the 1874 show. Her review set Morisot, the only woman exhibitor, beside a woman reviewer whom readers took for a man.

sources.title: Degas catalogue raisonné: Montifaud, 'Exposition du boulevard des Capucines' (1874)

add_eyes.name: 'Jean Prouvaire' (pseudonymous critic of Le Rappel)
add_eyes.role: Critic for the republican daily Le Rappel
add_eyes.where: Paris; the rooms at 35 boulevard des Capucines
add_eyes.authenticity: 'L'Exposition du boulevard des Capucines', Le Rappel, 20 April 1874. The pen-name is attributed to Catulle Mendès by some sources (the Ministère de la Culture cites 'Mendès', Le Rappel, 20 April) and to Pierre Toloza by others; the attribution is unsettled.
add_eyes.bio: Writing five days after the opening and five days before Leroy's satire, this critic treated the show as serious painting. The review is best remembered for its praise of Morisot's 'Le Berceau'. Because the author is unknown, the review can be judged only on what it says.

Ministère de la Culture: 1874, première exposition

add_eyes.name: Stéphane Mallarmé
add_eyes.role: Poet and English teacher, aged 32–34; Manet's close friend
add_eyes.where: Paris, rue de Moscou; writing for Paris and London
add_eyes.vantage_label: the poet arguing their case in print
add_eyes.language: French; the 1876 essay survives only in English
add_eyes.authenticity: 'Le Jury de peinture pour 1874 et M. Manet', La Renaissance artistique et littéraire, April 1874. 'The Impressionists and Edouard Manet', The Art Monthly Review and Photographic Portfolio (London), 30 September 1876, survives only in its English translation; the French manuscript is lost.
add_eyes.bio: Mallarmé saw Manet almost daily in these years. He defended him against the 1874 Salon jury and in 1876 explained the new painting to English readers. Of all the friendly writers he made the broadest claim for what the group meant.

sources.title: Nonsite: Morisot, early Impressionist criticism and the plein-air interior

add_eyes.name: Henry James
add_eyes.role: American writer, aged 33; Paris correspondent of the New York Tribune
add_eyes.where: Paris, rue de Luxembourg; writing for New York
add_eyes.vantage_label: a transatlantic critic in the rooms
add_eyes.authenticity: Paris letters to the New York Tribune, 1875–76. The piece on the second show ('Parisian Festivity', 13 May 1876) is collected in The Painter's Eye (ed. Sweeney, 1956) and Parisian Sketches (ed. Edel and Lind, 1957).
add_eyes.bio: James was in Paris to write fiction and paid his way with letters to the Tribune. He visited the second group show and was unimpressed. His verdict is the one in the chapter written in English for an American public, and it shows how far the group's ideas had yet to travel.

sources.title: Hannah, 'Henry James, impressionism and the public' (Rocky Mountain Review, 2007)

add_entries.date_display: April 1874 (day not verified; often given as 12 April)
add_entries.place: Paris, La Renaissance artistique et littéraire
add_entries.headline: A poet attacks the Salon jury for Manet
add_entries.digest: While the group hung their own show, Mallarmé took up the case of the friend who had stayed out of it. The Salon jury had taken one Manet and turned down two, and Mallarmé argued that a jury had no business shielding the public from a living painter. Two years later he would make the same argument at greater length, for the whole group.
add_entries.source_note: Mallarmé, 'Le Jury de peinture pour 1874 et M. Manet', as cited in the chapter's own Manet entry; day not verified

add_entries.headline: An early notice finds 'Le Berceau' true and tender
add_entries.digest: Five days into the show, Le Rappel's critic reviewed it as a real exhibition and not as a curiosity. He singled out Morisot's mother watching over a sleeping child, writing that nothing was truer or more tender. This was the kind of attention Guichard would soon tell her mother she could not afford to risk.
add_entries.source_note: Nonsite (Morisot and early criticism) cites Prouvaire on 'Le Berceau'; date and paper from the Ministère 1874 page (Le Rappel, 20 April, as 'Mendès'); attribution of the pen-name unsettled

add_entries.headline: A woman critic, writing as a man, walks the rooms
add_entries.digest: Montifaud reviewed the show for L'Artiste, the old-established art monthly. The Degas catalogue raisonné cites her review among those that discussed Degas. Reception studies remember her account of Cézanne's 'Une moderne Olympia' as an opium smoker's dream that the Sunday crowds jeered at. That description is summarised here from secondary accounts.
add_entries.source_note: Degas catalogue raisonné, bibliography 1281 (dated 9 May 1874); reviewer's note and other bibliographies give L'Artiste, 1 May 1874; content from secondary summaries, issue not consulted

add_entries.place: Paris, for the New York Tribune
add_entries.headline: Henry James finds the new school without virtue
add_entries.digest: In a Paris letter to the Tribune, James described the second group show at Durand-Ruel's to American readers. He found the painters had given up selection and arrangement, which to him was what made art. He summed up their doctrine as careless subjects carelessly painted. To him, that was not yet art.
add_entries.quote: a subject which has been crudely chosen shall be loosely treated
add_entries.source_note: 'Parisian Festivity', New York Tribune, 13 May 1876 (date per Parisian Sketches bibliography and reviewer's notes); phrases as quoted from The Painter's Eye, p. 115, in Hannah (2007), which loosely places the piece later in the year

add_entries.place: Paris, for The Art Monthly Review (London)
add_entries.headline: Mallarmé explains the Impressionists to London
add_entries.digest: Mallarmé's long essay 'The Impressionists and Edouard Manet' appeared in English in a London monthly. He treated Manet as the source of the open-air painting the group practised and gave Morisot a place of her own among them. He presented the new painting as an art suited to a modern, democratic public. The French text he wrote has never been found.
add_entries.source_note: The Art Monthly Review and Photographic Portfolio, 30 September 1876, as cited in Nonsite (Morisot and early criticism)

add_convergences.label: The first friendly notices (17–24 April 1874)
add_convergences.note: Before Leroy's joke had a name, two republican papers took the show seriously and praised Morisot by name. The critics' first reaction was not mockery. The mockery came a week later.

add_convergences.label: May 1874: the Salon opens and the reviews keep coming
add_convergences.note: As the Salon opened with one Manet on its walls, a woman critic writing as a man reviewed the independents in L'Artiste, and Pissarro told Duret the show was a success. The independents and the Salon were reviewed in the same weeks.

add_convergences.label: The second show crosses the Channel and the Atlantic (April–September 1876)
add_convergences.note: Burty explained the 'Intransigeants' to The Academy in April. James dismissed them to New York in May, and in September Mallarmé made the largest claim for them, in English, in London. All three were writing about the show at which Wolff had mocked Morisot as the woman among madmen.

add_ties.note: Mallarmé and Manet met almost daily in the 1870s; Manet painted his portrait in 1876, the year of the London essay.
Le Rappel's critic singled out 'Le Berceau' for praise on 20 April 1874.
Montifaud's review is remembered for its account of 'Une moderne Olympia' and the crowd's laughter (from secondary summaries).
In spring 1876 both explained the same show to English-speaking readers, Burty sympathetically in London and James dismissively in New York.

add_further.title: Nonsite: Berthe Morisot, early Impressionist criticism and the aesthetics of the plein-air interior

add_claims.evidence: Le Rappel, 20 April 1874, as cited by Nonsite and the Ministère de la Culture

add_claims.claim: Henry James dismisses the second group show in the New York Tribune
add_claims.evidence: 'Parisian Festivity', NY Tribune; reprinted in The Painter's Eye

add_claims.claim: 'The Impressionists and Edouard Manet' published in London in English; the French original is lost
add_claims.evidence: The Art Monthly Review and Photographic Portfolio, 30 September 1876

add_threads_out.note: In June 1889, during the Exposition Universelle, Monet showed alongside Rodin at the Galerie Georges Petit. That autumn he began the subscription to buy Manet's 'Olympia' for the nation. The painters of 1874 were now organising exhibitions of their own around an official world's fair.

fix.source_note: Ministère de la Culture 1874 page cites Burty, La République française, 24 April 1874, and quotes his remarks on the busy boulevard, the red-brown wool hangings and hanging by size and lot; Nonsite cites his 'Chronique du jour', La République française, 25 April 1874, praising Morisot's 'Cache-cache'; other studies give 16 April. Rest summarised from secondary accounts.
